title: What are the Schema Registry compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, NONE), how do they let producers and consumers deploy independently, and why does adding a new required field break compatibility unless you give it a default (so old data can still be read)?
shortTitle: Schema Registry compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, NONE) and why defaults matter

s1_definition.profdef: Schema Registry compatibility modes are rules the registry enforces when a new version of a schema is registered for a subject. BACKWARD means new consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous schema. FORWARD means old consumers using the previous schema can read data written with the new schema. FULL means both backward and forward hold. NONE disables checks entirely. These rules let producers and consumers be deployed and upgraded at different times without breaking each other. Adding a new field that is required breaks compatibility because old data has no value for it; giving the field a default makes it safe, because a reader can substitute the default when the field is absent.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps changing the transfer form. BACKWARD compatibility means a clerk trained on the new form can still read all the old filled forms in the archive. FORWARD means a clerk trained on the old form can still read a new form someone just filled in. FULL means both clerks can read both forms. NONE means nobody checks and chaos is allowed. Now, if the new form adds a mandatory "currency" box but every old archived form left it blank, the new clerk is stuck — there is no value. The fix is to print "INR" as the default in that box, so when the box is blank the clerk just assumes INR and keeps working.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compatibility modes let producers and consumers upgrade independently, and a new field is only safe to add if it has a default so old data remains readable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Schema Registry compatibility modes are rules the registry enforces when a new version of a schema is registered for a subject. BACKWARD means new consumers using the new schema can read data written with the previous schema. FORWARD means old consumers using the previous schema can read data written with the new schema. FULL means both backward and forward hold. NONE disables checks entirely. These rules let producers and consumers be deployed and upgraded at different times without breaking each other. Adding a new field that is required breaks compatibility because old data has no value for it; giving the field a default makes it safe, because a reader can substitute the default when the field is absent.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps changing the transfer form. BACKWARD compatibility means a clerk trained on the new form can still read all the old filled forms in the archive. FORWARD means a clerk trained on the old form can still read a new form someone just filled in. FULL means both clerks can read both forms. NONE means nobody checks and chaos is allowed. Now, if the new form adds a mandatory "currency" box but every old archived form left it blank, the new clerk is stuck — there is no value. The fix is to print "INR" as the default in that box, so when the box is blank the clerk just assumes INR and keeps working.

**One line to remember:** Compatibility modes let producers and consumers upgrade independently, and a new field is only safe to add if it has a default so old data remains readable.

sections.s2_technical:
The registry tracks schemas per subject, which is usually `topic-value`. Each time you try to register a new schema version, the registry compares it against existing versions using the subject's compatibility mode and rejects the registration if the rule is violated. This check happens at deploy or registration time, which is far better than discovering the break at runtime in production.

BACKWARD is the default and the most common in event systems. It means a consumer upgraded to the new schema can still read messages produced with the old schema. Safe backward changes are deleting a field and adding a field that has a default. You upgrade consumers first, then producers.

FORWARD means a consumer still on the old schema can read messages produced with the new schema. Safe forward changes are adding a field and deleting a field that had a default. Here you upgrade producers first, then consumers.

FULL means both directions must hold at once, so only the safest changes are allowed, essentially adding or removing fields that have defaults. There are also transitive variants, BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE and FORWARD_TRANSITIVE and FULL_TRANSITIVE, which check against all previous versions, not just the latest, which matters when consumers might read very old data.

NONE disables compatibility checking. It is occasionally used for a brand-new topic during early development, but in a bank it is dangerous because it allows breaking changes to ship silently.

The key rule about required fields: a field without a default is required. If you add a required field, then consider a consumer reading an old message that was written before the field existed. There is no value for the field and no default to fall back on, so decoding fails. That violates BACKWARD compatibility and the registry rejects it. The fix is to give the field a default, for example `"default":"INR"` for a currency field, so any reader encountering an old record without the field simply uses INR. In code, when you set the subject compatibility with the Confluent CLI or REST, you call something like `PUT /config/transfers-value {"compatibility":"BACKWARD"}`, and the Maven Avro plugin or `schema-registry-maven-plugin` can verify compatibility in CI so a bad schema fails the build.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a fraud service and a producer that both use the transfers schema. The teams release on different schedules. The fraud team wants to deploy a new schema version on Monday and the producer team on Thursday. Without a compatibility rule, whoever deploys first might break the other. This is exactly what BACKWARD compatibility solves — the registry guarantees the new consumer can still read old-schema records, so the deploys can happen in any order safely.

Problem 2 — A developer adds a mandatory `currency` field to the transfer schema. Every historical record in the topic was written before this field existed, so a new reader has nothing to put in `currency` and decoding would fail. This is exactly why a new required field breaks compatibility. The fix is to add the field with a default of INR, so old records decode by substituting INR.

We simulate the registry's compatibility check in plain Java. A `CompatChecker` compares an old field set with a new field set under a chosen mode and either accepts or rejects. The demo registers version 1, then tries to add a required field (rejected), then adds the same field with a default (accepted). The code will show: a `FieldDef` record, a `SchemaVersion`, the `CompatChecker` with BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL and NONE, and a demo that reproduces the required-field rejection and the default-field success.

```yaml
# application.yml — how you set the real registry compatibility mode
# Set per-subject via REST:
#   PUT http://localhost:8081/config/transfers-value  {"compatibility":"BACKWARD"}
spring:
  kafka:
    properties:
      schema.registry.url: http://localhost:8081
      auto.register.schemas: false   # register through CI, not silently at runtime
      use.latest.version: true
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: schema v1 with fromId, toId, amount, and two attempts at a v2 that adds currency.

Step 1: The subject `transfers-value` is set to BACKWARD. Version 1 has three required fields. All existing records on the topic match v1.

Step 2: A developer registers v2 that adds a required currency field. The checker walks the new fields, sees currency is new and has no default, and asks: can a new reader read an old v1 record? No, because old records lack currency and there is no default. It returns false and the registration is rejected.

Step 3: The developer fixes it by giving currency a default of INR. Now the checker sees currency is new but has a default, so an old record decoded by the new schema simply uses INR. It returns true and the registration succeeds as version 2.

Step 4: Because the mode is BACKWARD, the consumer team can deploy v2 first and keep reading all historical v1 records, then the producer team deploys v2 later. The deploys are independent.

Step 5: The demo also shows FULL accepts the default version and NONE accepts even the breaking version, illustrating why NONE is unsafe in a bank.

```
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [SEVERE ] REJECTED: adding required field 'currency' breaks BACKWARD compatibility — old records have no value for it.
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] currency with default INR under BACKWARD compatible=true
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] FULL check on v2Good=true
2026-10-24 20:50:21 [INFO   ] NONE always allows=true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Developer registers schema v2 for subject "transfers-value"
    │
    ▼
  Schema Registry (mode = BACKWARD)
    │ compare v2 against v1
    ├─ v2 adds REQUIRED currency ─────────→ REJECT (old data has no value)
    │        │ deploy fails in CI
    │        ▼
    │   developer adds default "INR"
    │
    └─ v2 adds currency WITH default INR ──→ ACCEPT as version 2
             │
             ▼
     Consumers deploy v2 first ──→ still read old v1 records (currency=INR)
     Producers deploy v2 later  ──→ write currency explicitly
     (independent deploy order, nothing breaks)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Compatibility Checker ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: CompatMode selects backward/forward/full/none rule     │
  │   WHY: Open/Closed — add a mode without rewriting the checker     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: CompatChecker only compares schemas; registry stores them     │
  │ O: new rule = new switch branch / strategy, existing code intact │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐
  │   CompatChecker       │───────▶│   SchemaVersion      │
  │  + isCompatible(mode, │ reads  │  - version: int      │
  │      old, new): bool  │        │  - fields: List      │◆──┐ owns
  │  - backwardOk(): bool │        │  + find(name):FieldDef│   │
  │  - forwardOk(): bool  │        └──────────────────────┘   ▼
  └───────────┬───────────┘                      ┌──────────────────┐
              │ uses                              │    FieldDef      │
              ▼                                   │  - name, type    │
        ┌───────────┐                             │  - hasDefault    │
        │ CompatMode│  BACKWARD|FORWARD|FULL|NONE │  + hasDefault()  │
        └───────────┘                             └──────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: schema registration ─────────────────────
  [PROPOSED] ──compat check──→ [REGISTERED v2]
       │                             ▲
       │ breaks rule                 │ add default / remove field
       ▼                             │
  [REJECTED] ───────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. checker.isCompatible(BACKWARD, v1, v2Bad)
  2.   → backwardOk: currency new, no default → false → REJECT
  3. checker.isCompatible(BACKWARD, v1, v2Good)
  4.   → backwardOk: currency new, has default → true → ACCEPT
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Schema Registry compatibility modes are the rules the registry enforces when someone registers a new version of a schema, and they are what let producers and consumers evolve on their own schedules without breaking each other. BACKWARD, which is the default, means a consumer on the new schema can still read messages written with the old schema, so you upgrade consumers first. FORWARD means a consumer still on the old schema can read messages written with the new schema, so you upgrade producers first. FULL requires both directions, so only the safest changes pass. NONE turns the checks off, which I avoid in a bank because it lets breaking changes ship silently.

The practical value is independent deployment. Because the registry guarantees the compatibility direction, the fraud team and the producer team can release on different days and in any order, and nothing breaks at runtime. The check runs at registration time, ideally in the CI pipeline through the schema registry Maven plugin, so a bad schema fails the build instead of failing a consumer in production.

The subtle point about required fields is the one interviewers probe. In Avro, a field without a default is required. If you add a required field, a consumer reading an older record that predates the field has no value to put there and no default to fall back on, so decoding fails and BACKWARD compatibility is violated, which is why the registry rejects it. The fix is simply to give the new field a default. For example, when we added a currency field we set its default to INR, so any old record without a currency decodes by substituting INR and keeps working.

In my banking platform at National Bank of India, we set every transfer topic to BACKWARD compatibility and register schemas through CI rather than auto-registering at runtime. When we needed to add a currency field, the first attempt made it required and the registry rejected it immediately, which saved us from a production incident. We added a default of INR and it registered cleanly, the consumers deployed first and kept reading years of historical records, and the producers rolled out later. The senior framing I give is that compatibility modes turn schema evolution from a coordinated, risky, big-bang release into a safe, independent, incremental process, which is exactly what you want across many teams sharing one banking event backbone.
